**Team Y · Boycotts and store visits at Target, 2023 and 2025**\
Lena Park, Marco Silva, Nadia Haddad, Owen Brooks, Priya Natarajan

## 1. Research question

Did the 2023 and 2025 boycotts of Target lower visits to its stores
most in the counties whose politics matched each boycott? This is an
evaluation. A retailer's marketing team, deciding where to spend on
promotions to win shoppers back after a boycott, would act on the
answer. The 2023 boycott came from conservative shoppers angry about
Pride merchandise, and the 2025 boycott from shoppers opposed to Target
ending its diversity goals. We expect visits to fall a few percent more
in Republican-leaning counties in 2023, and in Democratic-leaning
counties in 2025. We are wrong if visits fall by the same amount
everywhere, or if the same counties fall most in both years.

## 2. Why it matters

Both boycotts fell in quarters when Target's sales declined. Its
comparable store sales fell 4.3 percent in the second quarter of 2023
and 5.7 percent in the first quarter of 2025 (Target Corporation 2023,
2025). In 2023 the company said it could not separate the effect of the
reaction from other causes (Associated Press 2023b). If the losses
concentrate in counties whose politics match the boycott, a marketing
team can aim its promotions at those stores. If they do not, it spends
nationally. A retailer weighing a public stance could also estimate in
advance which stores it puts at risk, and for how long.

Two studies come closest to ours. Hou and Poliquin (2023) used phone
location data to count visits to the stores of several large retailers
whose chief executives backed expanding background checks for gun
purchases. Visits fell about 3 percent over four weeks, about 5 percent
in the most conservative counties and not at all in the most liberal
ones, and the drop faded within 10 weeks. Liaukonytė, Tuchman and Zhu
(2023) studied the boycott of Goya after its chief executive praised
President Trump. A counter-movement of supporters outweighed it. Sales
rose about 22 percent, and the rise was gone within three weeks. The
increase was largest in heavily Republican counties, with no strong
offsetting fall in heavily Democratic ones. Each study follows stances
on one side of politics. We study one retailer boycotted from opposite
sides two years apart, which lets us test whether the same stores move
in opposite directions.

## 3. Approach

Each observation is one Target store in one week. The outcome is the
logarithm of the store's weekly visits, from Advan's Weekly Patterns
Plus data in Dewey. The sample covers all of Target's nearly 2,000
stores in the United States, from January 2022 to December 2025, which
spans both boycotts. These are the stores a marketing team would choose
among.

The treatment is the boycott. Every store was exposed to it, so we
split stores by the politics of their county, measured by the
Republican share of the 2020 presidential vote. We compare stores in
the third of counties with the highest share against stores in the
third with the lowest. We date the 2023 boycott from the week of May
22, when Target pulled some Pride merchandise after confrontations in
its stores. The collection had drawn misleading videos for weeks before
that (Associated Press 2023a), so we leave out the weeks from its launch
in early May to May 22. We date the 2025 boycott from the week of
January 20, when Target announced it would end its diversity goals, and
we mark the 40-day boycott that began on March 5 (Hopkins and Gray News
staff 2025).

The comparison group for stores in the Republican third is the same
chain's stores in the Democratic third, and the reverse. Their visits
stand in for the counterfactual, what each group's visits would have
done without the boycott. Both groups share Target's prices, products
and national advertising, so anything the chain did to every store
drops out. The counties differ in income, density and much else, so we
compare each store's change in visits over time rather than its level.
The design is difference-in-differences, run as an event study for each
boycott. It compares the change in visits at stores in the Republican
third with the change at stores in the Democratic third, week by week,
from 20 weeks before each boycott to 20 weeks after. We make the
comparison among counties of similar income, so that a shock hitting
poorer counties does not show up as politics. This design measures how
much more visits fell in one group of counties than in the other. It
cannot measure the boycott's total effect on Target, because every store
was exposed. The identifying assumption is that, within each income
group and without the boycotts, visits in the two groups of counties
would have followed parallel paths.

The two boycotts also give us a check. If the boycotts drive the
response, the gap between the two groups should change sign between
2023 and 2025. A shock that hits the same counties in both years, such
as prices rising faster in poorer counties, would push the gap the same
way both times. A shift in spending that follows county politics could
flip it too, and section 5 explains how we separate that.

## 4. Data and access

| Dataset | Holder | Unit and period | Variables we need | Access time | Status |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Weekly Patterns Plus (Advan) | Dewey, through Cornell's subscription | Store-week, 2022–2025 | Brand, weekly visits, location | Days | File opened Oct 15 |
| County Presidential Election Returns 2000–2024 | MIT Election Data and Science Lab, public | County, each election | Republican share of the 2020 vote | Now | File opened Oct 12 |
| American Community Survey, 5-year estimates | U.S. Census Bureau, public | County, 2020–2024 | Median household income | Now | File opened Oct 12 |

We already hold all three datasets. If the visit data cover too few
stores in rural counties, the question narrows to stores in
metropolitan counties.

Weekly Patterns Plus counts visits to places and identifies no person,
which normally puts it outside IRB review. We do not get to make that
call ourselves, so we asked the IRB office on September 18. It confirmed
on October 9 that the project needs no application. We need no
data-use agreement, because we have no sponsor and the other two
sources are public. A retailer would pay for this answer, so if one
offered to sponsor the work, we would first ask whether Cornell's Dewey
licence allows commercial use.

## 5. Anticipated challenges

The main threat is omitted variables: a shift in spending that follows
county politics in the same weeks, with no boycott behind it. Our 2025
window opens in September 2024 and spans the presidential election and
the inauguration. If shoppers in Democratic-leaning counties cut
spending at every store after either event, Target's gap would move the
way the boycott predicts, and the sign check could not tell the two
apart. That would make our 2025 estimate too large. Visits to other
large chains in the same counties separate the two, because a boycott
of Target lowers visits at Target and a general cut lowers them
everywhere. We will use chains that sell different goods from Target
and took no public stance on diversity goals. If their gap moves the
same way as Target's, we will report by February 15 that our 2025
estimate cannot separate the boycott from a partisan shift in spending.

In 2023, Target moved its Pride merchandise to the back of some
Southern stores (Associated Press 2023a). If that softened the reaction
where conservative shoppers are concentrated, it pushes our 2023
estimate toward zero. We cannot observe which stores made the change,
so we will state it as a limitation in the outline by November 11.

## AI disclosure

**Tools.** ChatGPT (chatgpt.com).\
**Used for.** Suggesting search terms for studies of boycotts and store
visits. Suggesting how to date the start of each boycott.\
**Checked.** We opened both studies, Target's two earnings releases and
the three news reports, and confirmed every number and date we quote.
One study the tool suggested does not exist, and we dropped it. We put
no Dewey data into the tool.
